solver.kind: blind AI solver (separate agent, answer-free packet, rubric v2)

flags: minor: 'duplicate' and 'living' are throwaway distractors nobody would pick; only 'intact' is a real (antonym) lure, so the item comes down to two choices
S032-01.notes: A missing skull and tail means the specimen is incomplete, so 'fragmentary' fits. 'Intact' is the opposite. 'Duplicate' and 'living' make no sense in the sentence.

flags: minor: 'galvanized' is the only positive choice; the other three are all negative and are ruled out by the outcome (support grew, the bill passed)
S032-02.notes: Supporters who had wavered went on to commit and the bill passed, so the speech roused them to act. Alienated, bewildered and outnumbered all contradict that outcome.

flags: minor: C repeats the sentence's own 'Although ... long' contrast, so it is close to a paraphrase lookup
S032-03.notes: The third sentence explains why the wall is hard to see despite its length (it is narrow and close in color to the land around it). D is wrong because the final sentence extends that reasoning rather than rejecting a comparison. Facts check out: astronauts have confirmed the wall is hard to see from low orbit.

S032-04.notes: Bears carry salmon carcasses inland, and streamside leaves contain nitrogen typical of the ocean, so the salmon bring ocean nutrients to the forest. A (trees absorb ocean water directly) is unsupported. C changes the subject to bears' growth. D reverses the cause and effect. Facts are accurate: marine-derived N-15 in riparian trees and faster growth of Sitka spruce beside salmon streams (Reimchen; Helfield & Naiman).

flags: minor: C and D are written as fragments in a different style from A and B (a mild format cue)
S032-05.notes: A gap needs both measures for both groups. The gap is 45-38 = 7 points for ages 18-29 and 55-14 = 41 points for 65 and older. Only D gives all four numbers. A is the main trap: it covers only virtual tours. B covers only in-person visits, and C covers the wrong age group. Every number in the choices matches the table.

S032-06.notes: Text 2 says the rise works as a check that invites the listener to show they are following, even when the speaker is sure. That contradicts the critics' claim that it signals uncertainty. B distorts Text 2, C overgeneralizes from its examples, and D is not addressed in either text.

flags: minor: A is a plausible lure on the topic of delay but stresses the short wait; B and D are off-goal and easy to eliminate
S032-07.notes: The goal is to stress how long the ravens waited. C gives the longest delay (up to 17 hours) between choosing the tool and using it. Facts are consistent with Kabadayi & Osvath (2017, Science).

S032-08.notes: The second sentence qualifies the 'no emissions' claim, so a contrast transition is needed: 'Even so.' 'Therefore' (cause), 'Likewise' (similarity) and 'In other words' (restatement) all fail. The factual content is accurate.

S032-09.notes: The opening modifier 'Excavated...' must attach to the thing that was excavated, the body. A attaches it to the peat cutters and is also ungrammatical with 'so well preserved' following. C is an expletive construction with a dangling modifier. D attaches the modifier to the people and repeats 'the people who found it.' The facts are accurate: the Tollund Man was found by peat cutters in 1950, and the finders thought he was a recent murder victim.

S032-10.notes: Two independent clauses are joined by 'however', which needs a semicolon before it and a comma after it. A is a comma splice and B is a run-on. C omits the comma after 'however', which the SAT treats as an error.
